candidates.attacker_control: The access token string taken from the HTTP `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header of a request to an HTTP endpoint wired to the file-based OAuth2 authorization mechanism. The value is passed verbatim by the OAuth2 resource-server filter to AccessTokenResolver.resolve(context, token). RFC 6750 token characters (`A-Za-z0-9-._~+/` with optional `=`) permit both `.` and `/`, so a value containing `../..` segments is a syntactically plausible bearer token and reaches the un-normalised `new File(folderPath, token)` sink.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that: the file resolver is documented as 'should only be used for test purpose' and the mechanism is created disabled (Upgrade.java:519-527), so it is not on by default; `new File(parent, child)` does neutralise an absolute child path, so only `..` segments (and symlinks) escape, not `/etc/...`; the OAuth2 filter enforces required scopes and token expiry taken from the same JSON, so a planted file must contain matching fields; the final operations still go through the proxy-authz machinery (InternalProxyAuthzFilter / server-side PROXIED_AUTH + proxy ACI checks), limiting the blast radius; adjacent token resolvers were checked and found not injectable (CtsAccessTokenResolver uses DN.child("coreTokenId", token) whose AVA stores the value as a single escaped RDN; DnTemplate/DN.format and Filter.format escape their substitutions); the DSML servlet's XML handling and the LDAPServerFilter/SASL paths were also reviewed for a stronger remotely-triggerable sink and did not yield one.
candidates.impact: Filesystem path traversal from an HTTP-controlled string: the server opens and JSON-parses a file of the attacker's choosing outside the intended token directory (arbitrary file read is constrained to JSON-parseable content because of `Json.readJsonLenient`). When a suitable JSON file is available, the attacker-supplied file fully defines the request identity, scope set and expiry, so the request can be authenticated as an arbitrary identity resolvable by the configuration's IdentityMapper (e.g. `uid=<victim>`), i.e. authentication bypass/impersonation against the REST/LDAP gateway. Proxy-Authorization/PROXIED_AUTH checks on the internal connection remain in place at the server, so the achievable privilege level depends on that configuration, but the token-directory trust boundary is clearly broken.
candidates.prerequisites: (1) An HTTP endpoint (e.g. rest2ldap or admin endpoint) references a `ds-cfg-http-oauth2-file-authorization-mechanism` and that mechanism is enabled with an access-token-directory (the mechanism is created disabled by an upgrade task; the class Javadoc labels it test-purpose, so this is not the default deployment). (2) For the strongest impact, the attacker must be able to point the traversal at a JSON file whose content is attacker-influenced (or otherwise favourable) and that parses with `scope` (string array), `expireTime` (long) and the configured authzid JSON pointer field; writable directories (e.g. temp/shared volumes) or attacker-controlled adjacent JSON artefacts would satisfy this. Without such a file, the primitive is limited to reading/parsing chosen files and distinguishable success/failure behaviour.
candidates.root_cause: FileAccessTokenResolver.resolve() treats the client-supplied OAuth2 access token as a file name and concatenates it into a path with no confinement check: `new File(folderPath, token)` followed by `new FileInputStream(...)` (lines 49-55). Java's File(parent, child) strips leading separators from an absolute child but does not canonicalise or reject `..` components, so a token such as `../../../../<path>` escapes the configured `ds-cfg-oauth2-access-token-directory`. The file content is parsed as JSON and drives the resulting AccessTokenInfo: `scope`, `expireTime` and the authzid JSON pointer value that Authorization.createSecurityContextInjectionFilter() turns into `u:<value>` / `dn:<value>` in the SecurityContext, which server-legacy's InternalProxyAuthzFilter then resolves to an LDAP entry and uses as the authenticated identity for the request.
candidates.title: Path traversal in OAuth2 file-based access-token resolver via attacker-controlled Bearer token
candidates.trace: HTTP request with `Authorization: Bearer ../../../../<path>` -> Authorization.newConditionalOAuth2ResourceServerFilter (opendj-rest2ldap .../authz/Authorization.java:213-254) -> CHF ResourceServerFilter extracts the token and calls the resolver -> FileAccessTokenResolver.resolve (FileAccessTokenResolver.java:49-52) does `new FileInputStream(new File(folderPath, token))` -> `Json.readJsonLenient` parses the chosen file -> `new AccessTokenInfo(accessToken, token, scope, expireTime)` (lines 57-61) -> Authorization.createSecurityContextInjectionFilter (Authorization.java:256-275) writes `u:<authzid-pointer-value>` into the SecurityContext -> HttpOAuth2AuthorizationMechanism chains InternalProxyAuthzFilter (HttpOAuth2AuthorizationMechanism.java:99-104) -> InternalProxyAuthzFilter.filter (lines 68-80) resolves that identity through the configured IdentityMapper and returns an internal connection authenticated as that entry, so subsequent LDAP operations are performed as the identity named in the traversed file.
candidates.unverified: No runtime test was performed. The exact parsing/normalisation (or rejection) of the `Bearer` header value happens inside the external forgerock-http ResourceServerFilter, which is not part of this snapshot; I verified only that the resolver's contract receives the raw token string. Whether any real deployment enables the file-based OAuth2 mechanism, and whether an attacker can place/choose a JSON file with the required fields, is environment-dependent. Impact of impersonation also depends on the configured identity mapper, proxied-auth privileges and proxy ACIs.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22 Path Traversal (leading to arbitrary JSON file read/parse and potential authentication bypass/impersonation)

coverage_summary: Assigned tree: 4,667 model-visible source files; per get_source_scope there were 0 excluded binaries, 0 sensitive-name/symlink exclusions and 0 files over 5 MiB, so filtering did not remove any Java source. Per get_relation_scope the index is partial: 4,608 files indexed, 59 source files missing from the index, 1 parse error, 49,453 symbols/123,748 candidate edges; capabilities are syntax-only (containment, name/arity call and inheritance candidates, annotation-name hints) with control flow, data flow and semantic resolution explicitly not implemented, and no security oracle or findings loaded - no build/test run. I inspected, by targeted reading/search rather than exhaustively: HTTP/REST authorization paths (rest2ldap basic/simple/search/SASL/OAuth2 strategies and resolvers, DN/filter templates, token resolvers; server-legacy HTTP authz mechanisms, AllowDenyFilter, LDAPContextInjectionFilter, AdminEndpoint/Rest2LdapEndpoint), the DSML servlet, backup/restore and all zip-extraction code, JDBC/Cassandra storage backends, the Grizzly LDAP codec/ASN.1/TLS/SASL filters, ACI engine and IP address masks, task classes and their privilege checks, config persistence/permissions, LDIF/URL handling, and packaging scripts/Dockerfiles. Unreviewed or only search-sampled: most of the protocol/ldap and core operation code, replication/changelog, schema, plugin and monitor subsystems, large parts of opendj-core and opendj-config.
limitations: The P1 index has no data-flow/control-flow or semantic resolution, so the header-to-file-open path was established by reading source and API contracts, not by an index-proved flow.

The Bearer-token extraction/validation before the resolver lives in the external forgerock-http ResourceServerFilter, which is not in this snapshot; I could not verify whether it restricts token characters.
No builds, tests, scanners or exploits were run (per instructions); impact statements are static-analysis reasoning, and the candidate is an unconfirmed lead.
59 source files are missing from the relation index and were not systematically enumerated; the repository is ~48 MB of Java and only the areas listed in coverage were read in depth.
Deployment preconditions (file-based OAuth2 mechanism enabled, attacker ability to influence a JSON file on disk) cannot be verified from the repository snapshot alone.

rejected_leads.lead: Path traversal / zip-slip during backup restore: BackupManager.BackupArchiveReader.restoreZipEntry does `restoreDir.resolve(zipEntryName)` with no normalisation and `ensureFileCanBeRestored` only creates parent directories; archive integrity (cryptoEngine.check) is verified in restoreArchive only AFTER files have been written (BackupManager.java:1004-1021 vs 1098-1110).
rejected_leads.reason: Real missing containment check and post-write verification flaw, but exploiting it requires the ability to place a crafted archive (and matching backup info) in a backup directory the server will read, plus a backend-restore task/privilege; attacker control is filesystem/privileged rather than network-remote, so it is weaker than the submitted candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: StaticUtils.extractZipArchive writes zip entries as `new File(targetDirectory, entry.getName())` without canonical-path containment (StaticUtils.java:2517-2560).
rejected_leads.reason: Only reachable from EmbeddedDirectoryServer.setup with an archive supplied by the embedding application/build, not from remote input; local installer/embedded use only.

rejected_leads.lead: DSML servlet SOAP/XML parsing: the request body is parsed by a SAAJ MessageFactory (DSMLServlet.java:449) before JAXB unmarshalling; only the error path and the response document use the hardened createSafeXMLReader/createSafeDocument with FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING, disallow-doctype-decl and a SafeEntityResolver.
rejected_leads.reason: The hardened parsing/entity resolver is present for the repository-controlled paths, and the residual XXE risk depends on the JDK/container SAAJ implementation (outside this snapshot); cannot be verified from source alone.

rejected_leads.lead: Storage backends build SQL/CQL text from configuration values: jdbc/Storage.java and cassandra/Storage.java concatenate table/keyspace names derived from backend id / db-directory (cassandra Storage.java:156-162 uses a regex typo `[^a-zA-z0-9_]` that leaves backslash/backtick unescaped).
rejected_leads.reason: Values are administrator-controlled configuration, not attacker-controlled request data; data values are bound via PreparedStatement/bind variables, so no injection from LDAP content was found.

rejected_leads.lead: Packaging defaults: Dockerfile sets `ROOT_PASSWORD=${ROOT_PASSWORD:-"password"}` (line 11) and run.sh echoes the password to container logs (`echo "Password set to $PASSWORD"`, lines 31-32); setup.sh enables `allow-pre-encoded-passwords`.
rejected_leads.reason: Deployment/packaging hardening issues (default credential, password in logs) rather than an injection or access-control flaw in server code; noted for follow-up, not the strongest source-level candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Tasks without explicit privilege checks (e.g. SetGenerationIdTask keeps the upstream `FIXME -- Do we need any special authorization here?`; InitializeTask/InitializeTargetTask/PurgeConflictsHistoricalTask/ResetChangeNumberTask also have none).
rejected_leads.reason: Reaching these requires write access to cn=tasks (ACI-controlled administrative configuration), and comparisons show the file-based OAuth2 issue has direct request-level attacker control.

rejected_leads.lead: Grizzly LDAP transport / ASN.1 reader: negative/huge length handling in SaslFilter.handleRead (length from `message.getInt()` used unchecked) and LdapCodec length checks.
rejected_leads.reason: At worst malformed-input handling/DoS; no path to confidentiality/integrity impact was demonstrated and the BER reader has sequence-limit checks.

summary: Single strongest candidate: a path-traversal / token-directory-escape in the OAuth2 "file" access-token resolver (CWE-22), reachable from an HTTP `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header when an endpoint uses the shipped `ds-cfg-http-oauth2-file-authorization-mechanism`. `FileAccessTokenResolver.resolve()` builds the lookup path as `new File(folderPath, token)` and immediately opens it, without normalising the path or checking that it remains inside the configured token directory; the JSON read from that file then supplies `scope`, `expireTime` and the authzid used to build the request's `SecurityContext` (impersonation/authentication-decision impact). Other reviewed leads (backup-restore zip-slip, embedded-setup zip-slip, DSML XML parsing, storage backend identifier handling, Docker defaults) are noted as rejected/unconfirmed below. Per the task, the candidate is a lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.
